tier_reason: bench/results-corex/lz4-suite-corex.out (output of bench/b2bench.c) shows Blosc2 lz4+shuffle against memcpy on the same buffer, but it names no CPU model (host 'corex' only), compiler or flags, and it comes from the project itself, so it is first-party with partial methodology (C). The only comparison against plain zstd/lz4 found is an independent blog's directional statement, read in a search snippet only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: At 8 threads, lz4+shuffle clevel 1 (ratio 4.75): decompression 31337.5 MB/s vs memcpy(read) 8962.2 MB/s, and compression 13172.7 MB/s vs memcpy(write) 9641.2 MB/s (derived from page data: about 3.5x on decode and 1.4x on encode). At 16 threads, clevel 1: decomp 28495.0 MB/s and comp 19772.6 MB/s vs memcpy read 9311.2 / write 9828.8 MB/s (the 35428.1 MB/s figure is clevel 0, ratio 1.00, i.e. no compression). Single thread clevel 1 decode (5293.7 MB/s) is slower than memcpy(read) (8581.6 MB/s), and compression (2066.7 MB/s) is slower than memcpy(write) (4691.4 MB/s).
corrections.caveats: Result file is from Blosc 2.0.0.beta.6 (2020) with LZ4 1.9.3 and Zstd 1.4.9; CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated (first-party, tier C). The baseline is memcpy only: bench/ (b2bench.c, sum_openmp.c, sframe_bench.c, delta_schunk.c, zero_runlen.c and others) has no benchmark against standalone lz4/zstd/zlib, and the one README plot (images/Read-Partial-Slices-B2ND.png) compares the Python NDArray slicing (2.25/1.34/0.75/0.5 GB/s) against Zarr with Blosc1 and HDF5 via h5py-Blosc2, not against a codec. Data is synthetic. An independent blog (Aras Pranckevicius, 'Float Compression 8: Blosc', 2023) says, per a WebSearch snippet only (the site is blocked here), that Blosc defaults beat plain zstd (slightly higher ratio, faster compression, much faster decompression) and mostly beat plain lz4 (much better ratio, faster compression, slightly slower decompression); no numbers were read and its Blosc version is unconfirmed. The zstd sum_openmp output in the same folder shows compressed-in-memory summation slower than uncompressed (1582 MB/s vs 11818 MB/s at 1 thread). The Blosc2 blog, Blosc2-Debunking-Myths.pdf (blosc.org) and the SciPy NDim paper were blocked.

notes: The 8-thread numbers match the page. The 16-thread decompression figure in the record was the clevel 0 (uncompressed passthrough) row, so I corrected it to clevel 1. The license is BSD-3-Clause (3 clauses in LICENSE.txt), the repo has 586 stars and is not archived, and the last commit is 2026-10-01; all match. Tier C stands; a tier B upgrade would need the Aras blog's numbers from an environment that reaches aras-p.info.

tier_reason: The README has no numbers and only says the reimplementation is 'much slower than the original' Apple LZBITMAP with similar ratios; no benchmark exists in the repo.

corrections.caveats: No numeric comparison against lzfse, lz4 or any listed baseline; the README says it is much slower than Apple's original (closed-source) LZBITMAP, so it is a format-compatibility reimplementation, not a speed win. Built by reverse engineering via black-box testing. The last commit (2023-01-18, 'Add a license') is more than 3 years old; 11 commits, 58 stars. lzfse issue #62 only asks Apple to open-source LZBITMAP and has no numbers.

notes: Under the verifier rules this would be reject (not-faster / not-notable-tier-d); kept as confirm at tier D per the seed-record keep-and-document instruction, but the orchestrator may want decision keep with the shortcoming 'self-described slower than the original'. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 58 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2023-01-18, so maintenance_status corrected from stale to abandoned (>3 years before 2026-10-01).

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. The independent Search Benchmark, the Game (quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game) runs PISA 0.8.2 against Lucene 10.4.0 and Tantivy 0.26 with public code (engines/pisa-0.8.2: Dockerfile building with g++ on ubuntu:20.04, CMake Release with -march=native from its CMakeLists.txt) and a named CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D); results.json holds per-query timings. This is search-engine query latency against Lucene; it is not codec decode speed, and the record's codec claim itself remains tier D.

corrections.baseline: Lucene 10.4.0 (also Lucene 10.4.0 with BP doc reordering, and Tantivy 0.26) in the independent search-benchmark-game; the original codec baseline (StreamVByte / SIMD-BP128 inside PISA) has no published numbers
corrections.workload: Search Benchmark, the Game (quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game, results.json from commit 'use Docker to build pisa, update results', 2026-05-31): English Wikipedia, AOL-derived queries run single-threaded as term/intersection/union/negated/intersection_union queries under TOP_10, TOP_100, TOP_1000, TOP_100_COUNT and COUNT collectors, best of 10 runs per query, warm page cache. PISA 0.8.2 uses FastPFOR blocks of 128, block-max WAND, and doc IDs reordered by recursive graph bisection; it ran 661 of the queries (no phrase queries, which have empty timings).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Over the 661 queries PISA ran, geometric-mean speedup of per-query best time vs Lucene 10.4.0 (derived from page data): TOP_10 1.04x, TOP_100 1.43x, TOP_1000 2.19x, TOP_100_COUNT 2.17x, COUNT 0.56x (slower). Vs Lucene 10.4.0 with BP reordering: 0.80x, 1.04x, 1.57x, 1.68x, 0.43x. Vs Tantivy 0.26: 1.44x, 1.60x, 2.14x, 1.70x, 0.58x. Mean of per-query best times (us), PISA vs Lucene 10.4.0 (derived from page data): TOP_10 495 vs 346, TOP_100 641 vs 536, TOP_1000 823 vs 998, TOP_100_COUNT 1586 vs 2737, COUNT 1564 vs 307. The repo README separately cites the ECIR 2019 study: average latency 10-40 ms (top 10) and 20-50 ms (top 1000) on 50M web documents, with no baseline.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ from Ubuntu 20.04 apt build-essential (GCC 9 series implied by the image; the exact version is not printed), CMake 3.21.3, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -march=native, C++17 (search-benchmark-game engines/pisa-0.8.2/Dockerfile and CMakeLists.txt)
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Manjaro Linux, kernel 7.0.3-1-MANJARO (search-benchmark-game README environment for results.json)
corrections.caveats: The win is mixed and collector-dependent: PISA is faster than Lucene on TOP_1000 and TOP_100_COUNT, roughly even on TOP_10 by geometric mean but slower by mean latency, and about 2x slower on COUNT; Lucene with BP reordering beats it on TOP_10 and COUNT. PISA does not run phrase queries in the suite. These are whole-engine query-latency numbers versus Lucene, not codec decode-speed numbers versus StreamVByte/SIMD-BP128; no per-codec table exists in the PISA repo (benchmarks/ has index_perftest.cpp, perftest_interpolative.cpp and scan_perftest.cpp but no published output). Results were run by the Tantivy maintainers (PSeitz); the suite UI switched to average timings on 2026-09-05, while these figures use best-of-10 per query. The ECIR 2019 paper (Springer), OSIRRC paper (ceur-ws) and pisa-engine.github.io docs were blocked. PISA is a fork of ot/ds2i, which is already a wave 9 integer-bitpacking entry.

notes: I found an independent tier A source: search-benchmark-game results.json has PISA 0.8.2 timings with public build files and a named CPU. The geometric means are my own computation from results.json. The comparison is engine-level against Lucene, so the orchestrator should consider overriding category to text-search-and-indexing (wave 3 lists Tantivy, SereneDB/IResearch and SeekStorm against Lucene, and its batch-05 record already references PISA 0.8.2 in this suite). Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0, 1.1k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-20 ('Fix CI-build, dockerfiles (#643)').
